items: List every project in a document with the project name, start date, hours invested, and income generated so far so you can see the full scope of what you're juggling.
Categorize each project as Active and promising, Idle but might return, or Dead project based on whether you're working on it and whether it shows revenue potential.
Calculate the total hours invested across all projects and the total income generated to reveal the true cost of staying in the starting loop instead of finishing anything.
Identify whether your projects cluster in one category like e-commerce, content creation, or freelance services because clustered projects share skills and audiences that can compound.
Evaluate each project against four criteria: revenue proof, time to market under 30 days, skill leverage, and emotional pull to find the one that passes at least three of them.
Move all non-chosen projects to an Archive folder, not Paused, so they leave your mental to-do list completely and stop pulling at your attention.
For each archived project, write down why you started it, why you stopped, and what you learned to turn abandonment into valuable information instead of wasted effort.
Apply the motorcycle app test by imagining your projects are desk drawers and noticing which one you would open first in the morning to find your real project.
Set a daily alarm for 60 minutes before your day job and protect that time from phone, social media, and email to build your side hustle muscle consistently.
Pick one metric to improve each week such as revenue, email subscribers, or lead inquiries and rotate through your most important numbers to prevent overwhelm while creating clear weekly goals.
Write down everything you did NOT do each Friday to practice the uncomfortable skill of deciding what not to work on, which builds comfort with letting go.
Share your one chosen project with one trusted person who will ask you about it weekly to create enough accountability to keep you honest without requiring public commitment.
